Where a claimant is entitled to a national social security benefit by virtue of falling within the scope of Council Directive 79/7/EEC, does Community law, in the circumstances of the present case, entitle the claimant to interest on the award of benefit and, if so: (i)from what date is interest payable,(ii)what shall the rate of interest be, (iii) is interest to be calculated only on the balance which falls due after off-setting, in accordance with national overlapping rules, any other benefit payments made from the same period?
position: Community law does entitle a claimant to interest on an award of arrears of a benefit made pursuant to a directly enforceable right to equal treatment conferred by Directive 79/7/EEC. The interest should be calculated so as to achieve the underlying objective of Directive 79n, namely, the restoration of real equality of treatment, and should be at a rate and for a period calculated by the national authorities or court to achieve that objective. It should be calculated on a basis which takes account of any other benefits which were in fact paid because of the failure to pay the benefit wrongly withheld.

position: It depends on the contract of the commercial agent with the principal. If the principal grants the commercial agent an exclusive right and a right to a commission for each supply made in the geographical area, the commercial agent is entitled to the commission. legal_issue: Is the Court second seised required or permitted, for the purpose of deciding whether or not to decline jurisdiction in respect of, or to stay, the proceedings before it, to conduct any and, if so, what examination of the basis upon which the court first seised assumed jurisdiction?
position: the question whether the court second seised may exercise jurisdiction must be governed by its domestic conflict rules relating to concurrent proceedings. Nevertheless, from the time of the entry into force of the Brussels Convention between the two States concerned, Article 29(2) of the San Sebastian Convention may impose an ohligation, in relation to a judgment given after the date of the entry into force of the Convention, to recognise and enforce such a judgment if the jurisdiction of the State of origin was founded on rules which accorded with the jurisdictional provisions of the Brussels Convention or with the provisions of a convention which was in force between the State of origin and the State addressed when the proceedings were instituted. In those circumstances, the court second seised should be able, for the purpose of deciding whether or not to decline jurisdiction in respect of the proceedings before it, to examine the basis on which the court first seised assumed jurisdiction. If the exercise of jurisdiction by the State first seised accords with the Brussels Convention rules on jurisdiction, it would normally be inopportune for the State second seised to exercise jurisdiction.

legal_issue: Is the Court second seised required or permitted, for the purpose of deciding whether or not to decline jurisdiction in respect of, or to stay, the proceedings before it, to conduct any and, if so, what examination of the basis upon which the court first seised assumed jurisdiction?
position: The court second seised must apply Article 21 of the latter Convention if the court first seised has assumed jurisdiction on the basis of a rule which accords with the provisions of Title II of that Convention or with the provisions of a convention which was in force between the two States concerned when the proceedings were instituted, and must do so provisionally if the court first seised has not yet ruled on whether it has jurisdiction. position: In principle, it must be calculated solely on the basis of the cost of the service or operation for which it constitutes the conterpart but for the purpose of setting fees, a Member State shall apportion its total registration fees between different categories of operations, each category grouping together operations which are similar in terms of the staff required, the duration of the procedure and the administrative costs. The Member State may then allocate the total relevant expenditure between the different categories on the basis of a reasonable estimate of the funds needed to carry out the operations of each category. If it proves difficult to determine the costs of a particular operation, a Member State is also entitled to fix in advance a lump sum calculated on the basis of the average cost of that category of operations. Member States are required to verify, at the end of each financial year, that the fees fixed without time limit do not exceed the costs of the operation for which they are the counterpart.

position: Yes, only where it is established that the charge has been borne in its entirety by another person and that reimbursement of the trader would constitute unjust enrichment. It is for the national courts to determine, in the light of the facts in each case, whether those conditions have been satisfied. If the burden of the charge has been passed on only in part, it is for the national authorities to reimburse the trader the amount not passed on. position: The semantic content is irrelevant in this case: The two signs are graphically sufficiently similar in order to qualify a likelihood of confusion.

legal_issue: Under Directive 89/104, is it sufficient, in order to find that there is a likelihood of confusion between a sign resulting from the combination of a word and a picture and a sign which, although registered for identical and similar goods, has been registered only as a picture and is not particularly well known to the public, that the two pictures coincide in their semantic content?
position: No, there is a likelihood of confusion, including a likelihood of association, when, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, and in particular the distinctive character of the trade mark, the trade mark and the sign, taken together and in their mutual relationship, are visually, phonetically or conceptually similar to each other to such an extent as to create a likelihood of direct or indirect confusion, as well as a likelihood of association.

legal_issue: Are the disputed charges, which have the characteristics of a tax, contrary to Article 95 of the Treaty of Rome?
position: A parafiscal charge, applicable without distinction to domestic and imported products, constitutes a charge having equivalent effect to a customs duty, prohibited by Article 12 of the EC Treaty, where the resources deriving from it are devoted in their entirety to the financing of advantages which benefit domestic products exclusively and thus fully offset the burden on them. If, on the other hand, the resources in question have been only partially allocated to such advantages and if they have offset only part of the burden on national products, the tax in question constitutes a discriminatory charge prohibited by Article 95 of the Treaty. This is for the national court to determine.

position: No, but the proprietor may prohibit the removal and re-application of his mark to the goods where he has legitimate reasons for objecting to the further marketing of the goods in that form, i.e. where the use of the mark is likely to adversely affect the reputation of the mark or call into question the guarantee of origin and thus prejudice the specific purpose of the mark.  This exemption shall apply only where the court has clear and unambiguous evidence that the nature of the removal and reapplication of the mark is such as to be detrimental to the reputation of the mark or to call into question the warranty of origin. The existence of such evidence is a question of fact for the national court to determine.

position: The concept of "habitual residence" under Article 8(1) of the Regulation must be interpreted as meaning that it corresponds to the place which reflects some degree of integration by the child in a social and family environment. To that end, in particular the duration, regularity, conditions and reasons for the stay on the territory of a Member State and the family’s move to that State, the child’s nationality, the place and conditions of attendance at school, linguistic knowledge and the family and social relationships of the child in that State must be taken into consideration. It is for the national court to establish the habitual residence of the child, taking account of all the circumstances specific to each individual case.

legal_issue: How is the concept of habitual residence to be interpreted in Community law?
position: The habitual residence is located at the place where there is a non-temporary stay, where the childs center of life is located; for this purpose, all circumstances of the case must be taken into account, especially the childs social integration and the existence of social or family or other links. It is not important that the stay is frequent or that there is a legal residence. The assessment of the jurisdiction based on Article 8(1) of the Regulation must be carried out, when the national court acts on its own motion, on the day that the jurisdiction is first seized in the sense of Article 2(1) of the Regulation. According to Article 12 of the Regulation, jurisdiction based on Article 13(1) of the Regulation implies the impossibility of establishing the habitual residence. This stops when habitual residence is acquired in one State.

legal_issue: How is the concept of habitual residence to be interpreted in Community law?

Is national legislation that permits the diversion of water from a particular river basin to another river basin, without the plans having yet been drawn up for the river basin districts within which the river basins are located, consistent with the Water Framework Directive?
position: It does not preclude, in principle, a provision of national law whereby consent is given, prior to 22 December 2009, to a transfer of water from one river basin to another or from one river basin district to another where the management plans for the river basin districts concerned were not yet adopted by the competent national authorities. Such a transfer must not be such as seriously to jeopardise the realisation of the objectives laid down by that directive. However, to the extent that that transfer is liable to have adverse effects on water of the kind stated in Article 4(7) of that directive, consent may be given to it, at the very least if the conditions set out in Article 4(7)(a) to (d) are satisfied.

legal_issue: Should the preceding question be answered in the affirmative: For the purpose of Articles 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 13 and 15 of Directive 2000/60, is the transfer of water from a river basin district to a neighbouring river basin district permitted? Should the answer be in the affirmative, can the purpose of that transfer be only to meet water-supply needs or can irrigation and power generation also be served? Is it in any event a requirement, for the purpose of those provisions of that directive, that the administrative authorities have decided, stating reasons and on the basis of the necessary scientific study, that the receiving river basin district cannot meet with its own water resources the needs which it has in respect of water supply, irrigation and so forth?
position: Yes, the authorisation of the diversion of waters from one river basin district to a neighbouring river basin district is compatible with the Water Framework Directive if it satisfies the conditions under Article 4(1), (7), (8) and (9) of the Water Framework Directive. Under Article 4(7)(c) of the Water Framework Directive, the objectives of drinking water supply, irrigation and power generation may justify measures which are inconsistent with the environmental objectives under Article 4(1) where the contribution made by those measures to achieving those objectives outweighs the adverse effect on the environmental objectives.

Under [Directive 2003/4], where a public authority holds environmental information, disclosure of which would have some adverse effects on the separate interests served by more than one exception (in casu, the interests of public security served by Article 4(2)(b) and those of intellectual property rights served by Article 4(2)(e)), but it would not do so, in the case of either exception viewed separately, to any extent sufficient to outweigh the public interest in disclosure, does the Directive require a further exercise involving the cumulation of the separate interests served by the two exceptions and their weighing together against the public interest in disclosure?
position: Where a public authority holds environmental information or such information is held on its behalf, it may, when weighing the public interests served by disclosure against the interests served by refusal to disclose, in order to assess a request for that information to be made available to a natural or legal person, take into account cumulatively a number of the grounds for refusal set out in that provision.

position: Where a public authority holds environmental information, disclosure of which would have some adverse effects on the separate interests served by more than one exception under Article 4(2), but it would not do so, in the case of either exception viewed separately, to any extent sufficient to outweigh the public interest in disclosure, the directive requires a further exercise involving the cumulation of the separate interests served by the two exceptions and their weighing together against the public interest in disclosure.

position: In the case of a merger operation between two companies of the same group the acquired company does not carry out any activity, does not have any financial holdings and transfers to the acquiring company only substantial tax losses of undetermined origin, even though that operation has a positive effect in terms of cost structure savings for that group, may constitute a presumption that the operation has not been carried out for ‘valid commercial reasons’ within the meaning of Article 11(1)(a). position: No. Recipients of old age pensions, to whom the legislation of several Member States applied, but whose pension are based on the legislation of the former Member State of employment alone, are entitled to claim from the competent authorities of that State the full amount of the family allowances provided under that legislation for handicapped children, even though they have not, in the Member State of residence, applied for comparable, higher, allowances under the legislation of that latter State, because they opted to be granted another benefit for handicapped persons which is incompatible with those, since the right to family allowances in the former Member State of employment was acquired by reason of the legislation of that State alone.

It precludes the adoption, by a Member State, of standards applicable to the transport by road of pigs defining in greater detail the requirements provided for by that regulation in respect of access to animals in order to check regularly their welfare conditions, which relate only to journeys of more than eight hours’ duration; and it does not preclude the adoption, by a Member State, of standards according to which, where pigs are being transported by road, the animals must have a minimum surface area which varies according to their weight, that surface area being, for a 100 kg animal, 0.42 m2 where the journey time is less than eight hours and 0.50 m2 for journeys of more than eight hours.

What are the criteria in law to be applied by a competent authority to an assessment of the likelihood of a plan or project the subject of Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive, having "an adverse effect on the integrity of the site"?
position: The Directive requires a consideration of the implications of a proposed plan or project for the conservation objectives of a site meaning : if the site concerns the preservation and maintenance of a non-renewable Annex I priority natural habitat type, and if the project in question requires the permanent destruction of a part of that habitat. If the proposed project removes part of that habitat, it adversely affects the integrity of that site and, therefore, requires consideration according to the criteria set out in Article 6(4) of the Habitats Directive. This is the prudent path to take in light of the precautionary principle.

legal_issue: What are the criteria in law to be applied by a competent authority to an assessment of the likelihood of a plan or project the subject of Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive, having "an adverse effect on the integrity of the site"?
position: If the project relates to construction within a site, the proportion of the site taken for the construction; if a proportion of a site is taken for construction, the extent to which that proportion involves the removal of any habitat for which the site is designated; the degree of fragmentation (if any) caused by the project; the impact of such fragmentation on the habitat and the species for which the habitat is designated; the impact of the project on the structural coherence of the habitat and its ability to continue to function as a habitat; if there has been a previous project or projects carried out on or in the vicinity of the site, the relationship between the impacts of the project and the impacts of any earlier project;  and the ability of mitigation measures to reduce any of the above impacts.

legal_issue: What are the criteria in law to be applied by a competent authority to an assessment of the likelihood of a plan or project the subject of Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive, having "an adverse effect on the integrity of the site"?
position: The Directive requires a consideration of the implications of a proposed plan or project for the conservation objectives of a site. Where the objective scientific conclusion is that the project will have a localised severe impact and severe negative impact, this could only lead to a negative assessment of the implications for the site and necessarily constitutes an adverse effect on the integrity of the site. Measures intended merely to reduce the area or scale of an adverse effect (in contrast to measures which avoid such an adverse effect entirely) cannot alter a conclusion (where such is reached) that the project will adversely affect the integrity of the site concerned.

Does the application of the precautionary principle have as its consequence that a plan or project cannot be authorised if it would result in the permanent nonrenewable loss of the whole or any part of the habitat in question?
position: Competent authorities may authorise a project under Article 6(3)  of the Habitats Directive only if they have made certain that it will not adversely affect the integrity of that site. That is the case where no reasonable scientific doubt remains as to the absence of such effects. It is never open to a competent authority to authorise the loss of an entire site. The question of whether the loss of a particular portion of a site adversely affects the integrity of a site is one to be assessed on a case-by-case basis by the competent authority. The fact that the habitat in question may be non-renewable is irrelevant to this inquiry.

position: The Internet can be defined as a collection of thousands of different networks, servers, computers and devices from all over the world, which communicate with each other using the IP protocol and route data packets between them. The Internet is a global information space and serves as the physical basis for the World Wide Web and many other data transmission protocols that provide a wide range of information services.

legal_issue: What is meant by Internet within the meaning of the Explanatory Notes to the CN for a good to be classified under code 8528 71 13?

The Internet is understood to be a medium, i.e. technologies, means of transmission and equipment, in which, in the context of interactive information exchange, the client can send e-mails or messages using, for example, a TCP/IP interface. The notion of "Internet" would therefore refer to the standard TCP/IP protocol package which uses the global system of Intemet, i.e. interactive communication and the possibility of opening Internet applications in the current sense.

legal_issue: Does Article 79(1) of Regulation 1408/71 infringe the general principles of equality and non-discrimination enshrined, inter alia, in Article 14 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms read in conjunction with Articles 17, 39 and/or 43 of the consolidated version of the EC Treaty, when interpreted as allowing only the deceased parent to benefit from the rules on the assimilation of periods of insurance, employment or self-employment set out in Article 72?
position: Article 79(1) of Regulation No 1408/71 does not limit the application of the principles of aggregation of insurance periods and aggregation of facts to the deceased parent alone in the circumstances of the present case, where the national legislation, determined pursuant to Article 78(2)(b)(i), provides for special family benefits for orphans under Chapter 8 of the Regulation and makes eligibility for that benefit conditional upon receipt of another work-based family benefit during the requisite qualifying period immediately preceding the death of the deceased parent. In accordance with the provisions of national law, these conditions of eligibility may also be satisfied in respect of the surviving parent who assumes responsibility for the orphaned child and who applies for the granting of this benefit, by taking into account, to the extent necessary, the periods of insurance and employment completed by the latter in the territory of another Member State, as provided for in Article 72 of Regulation No 1408/71.

legal_issue: Does Article 79(1) of Regulation 1408/71 infringe the general principles of equality and non-discrimination enshrined, inter alia, in Article 14 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms read in conjunction with Articles 17, 39 and/or 43 of the consolidated version of the EC Treaty, when interpreted as allowing only the deceased parent to benefit from the rules on the assimilation of periods of insurance, employment or self-employment set out in Article 72?
position: Where the national legislation of a Member State provides that a right to benefits for orphans can be established by both the deceased parent and the surviving parent, provided that they have the status of employed persons, those provisions of European Union law require that periods of insurance and employment completed by the surviving parent in another Member State be taken into account in the aggregation of the periods necessary to acquire the right to benefits in the first of those Member States. In that regard, it is not relevant that the surviving parent cannot rely on any period of insurance or employment in that Member State during the reference period laid down by that national legislation for the acquisition of that right.

Where it appears that a producer who has received Community aid for the storage of concentrated grape must in return for concluding a storage contract with the national intervention agency has acquired the grape must from a fictitious or non-existent company and then had it concentrated under his responsibility before storing it, can he be regarded as the owner of the concentrated grape must within the meaning of Article 2(2) of Regulation No 1059/83?
position: Whether a producer can be regarded as the owner of a product in circumstances such as those in the present case depends on the national rules on the ownership of goods applicable in such a situation. It is for the national court to refer to those rules in order to assess whether this is the case here. In the alternative, a producer cannot be regarded as the owner of a product which is the subject of a storage contract within the meaning of Article 2(2) of Regulation No 1059/83 where, owing to the non-existent or fictitious nature of the company from which he acquired that product, he is unable to establish his right of ownership over it.

Where an economic operator has failed to fulfil the obligations laid down by a sectoral Community regulation, such as Regulation No 1059/83, and the conditions laid down therein for entitlement to Community aid, and where that sectoral regulation provides, as in the case of Article 17 of the above mentioned regulation, for a system of measures or penalties, does that system apply to the exclusion of any other system provided for by European Union law, even though the failure in question is detrimental to the financial interests of the European Union? Or is the system of administrative measures and penalties provided for in Regulation No 2988/95, on the contrary, the only one applicable in the case of such an infringement? Or are both regulations applicable?
position: The provisions of Article 4 of Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 2988/95 are no longer applicable to a specific sectoral regulation such as Article 17 of the sectoral Regulation (EEC) No 1059/83. But they are again applicable: either when the sectoral regulation does not provide for any measure; or when the sectoral regulation does not provide for any measure for certain irregularities when the protection of Community funds requires it; this is the case when particularly serious defects affect the very existence of long-term storage contracts which do not fall within the scope of Article 17 of the sectoral regulation.
